\chapter{Two Actions, One Clause}
\label{ch:hi-chained-actions}
\hlchaptermodality{73}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can chain two actions inside a single Hindi clause with -kar, conjugating only the last verb.}

Complete HI-R73-chain and say the same two actions twice -- joined with aur, then chained with -kar -- and count the person endings in each.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[-kar]{-\hi{कर} (\emph{-kar}) — having done it}

\label{lesson:HI-C73-kar}



\begin{quote}
Say the \textbf{\hi{जब} … \hi{तब}} frame. Two clauses, two verbs, a word at each end. That is a lot of scaffolding for \emph{first this, then that} — and Hindi has a much shorter way that it uses far more often.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: put -\hi{कर} on the stem and the clause disappears}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\hi{मैं} \hi{किताब} \hi{देखकर} \hi{आता} \hi{हूँ}.} — \emph{maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ.} — \textbf{I look at the book and come.} (Literally: \emph{having looked, I come.})
\end{quote}

The move is the same shape as \textbf{\hi{सकना}}: \textbf{take the -\hi{ना} off the first verb and put -\hi{कर} on the bare stem.}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\hi{देखना}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{देखकर}} — having looked
  \item \textbf{\hi{करना}} $\to$ \textbf{\hi{करके}} — having done (this one is irregular, and it is the commonest of all)
\end{itemize}

What you get is not a second clause. It is one clause with a chained action inside it, and only the LAST verb takes a person ending. That is why Hindi reaches for it constantly: a speaker can string three actions together and conjugate once.

The order is the order of events. \textbf{\hi{देखकर} \hi{आता} \hi{हूँ}} is look-then-come, never the other way round, so you say the actions in the sequence they happen.

The ending is the verb \textbf{\hi{करना}} frozen solid. \emph{Having looked} is literally \emph{look-do}. Marathi does the same job with its own \emph{-ūn}; both languages inherited the construction from Sanskrit and each reinforced it with its own material.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{dekhnā} $\to$ \emph{dekhkar}, then \emph{karnā} $\to$ \emph{karke}
  \item \emph{maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ}
  \item which of the two verbs carries the person ending — \textbf{the last one}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \textbf{-\hi{कर}} attach to? (\textbf{The bare stem, after the -\hi{ना} comes off}.) How many verbs in a \textbf{-\hi{कर}} sentence take a person ending? (\textbf{One — the last}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%95\%E0\%A4\%B0}{Wiktionary: \hi{कर}}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[… -kar …]{One clause or two}

\label{lesson:HI-R73-chain}



\begin{quote}
You now have three ways to put two actions in one sentence: \emph{aur} between two clauses, the \textbf{\hi{जब} … \hi{तब}} frame, and \textbf{-\hi{कर}} inside a single clause. Only one of them conjugates just once.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{maiṁ kitāb dekhtā hūṁ aur ātā hūṁ} — two endings
  \item \emph{maiṁ kitāb dekhkar ātā hūṁ} — one ending
  \item which of the two a Hindi speaker says more often — \textbf{the -\hi{कर} one}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many person endings does a \textbf{-\hi{कर}} sentence carry? (\textbf{One}.) And an \emph{aur} sentence with two verbs? (\textbf{Two}.) Then stop.
\end{tcolorbox}
